questions.prompt: An ideal gas expands isothermally into a larger available volume. What is the sign of its entropy change?
options: Negative, because the gas becomes less dense
Zero, because temperature is constant
Positive, because the particles can be dispersed through more space.
Impossible to discuss unless gas molecules break apart
questions.explanation: C is correct. Greater accessible volume permits more spatial arrangements at the same temperature. A is incorrect: lower density during expansion corresponds to greater dispersal. B is incorrect: volume can change entropy even at fixed temperature. D is incorrect: entropy can change without a chemical reaction.

questions.prompt: Water vapor condenses to liquid at the same transition temperature. What happens to the entropy of the water sample?
options: It decreases.
It increases because attractions become stronger
It remains unchanged because the molecules stay H2O
It must become negative in absolute value
questions.explanation: A is correct. The particles become much less spatially dispersed in the condensed phase. B is incorrect: stronger constraints in the liquid do not imply more dispersal. C is incorrect: entropy can change in a physical process. D is incorrect: a negative entropy change does not mean negative absolute entropy.

questions.prompt: What best explains the positive entropy change when an ordinary crystalline solid melts?
options: Every intramolecular covalent bond must break
Particles gain access to more arrangements and freedom of motion.
The particles lose all motion in the liquid
The substance necessarily produces more atoms
questions.explanation: B is correct. The liquid is less constrained than the ordered crystal, increasing matter and energy dispersal. A is incorrect: melting a molecular solid need not destroy its molecules. C is incorrect: liquid particles continue moving. D is incorrect: melting conserves atom inventory.

questions.prompt: A gas sample is heated at fixed volume without reacting. Why does its entropy generally increase?
options: Every particle acquires exactly the same speed
Heating must compress the gas into a smaller spatial volume
Its entropy can change only if volume also increases
Energy is distributed among a wider range of accessible particle energies.
questions.explanation: D is correct. The broader energy distribution increases the ways energy can be dispersed. A is incorrect: thermal speeds remain distributed. B is incorrect: the volume is explicitly fixed, so the entropy increase must not be attributed to compression. C is incorrect: temperature changes can alter entropy independently.

questions.prompt: Which qualitative entropy trend is expected for2NO2(g) → N2O4(g)?
options: A decrease, consistent with fewer gas molecules.
An increase because the product formula is longer
No change because nitrogen and oxygen atoms are conserved
An increase because one molecule always has more entropy than two molecules
questions.explanation: A is correct. Association reduces total gas moles from two to one, generally reducing matter dispersal. B is incorrect: formula length is not the relevant gas inventory criterion. C is incorrect: atom conservation does not force equal entropy. D is incorrect: the reaction compares stoichiometric totals, not a single molecule in isolation.

questions.prompt: For CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g), what sign is generally expected for the reaction entropy change?
options: Negative because there are fewer product species
Zero because the equation is balanced
Positive, because gas is produced from initially solid material.
Always negative whenever a solid remains
questions.explanation: C is correct. The newly available gaseous particles give much greater dispersal. A is incorrect: there are two product species, and gas production is the dominant qualitative clue. B is incorrect: balancing conserves atoms, not entropy. D is incorrect: a remaining solid does not negate the entropy contribution from gas production.

questions.prompt: Ice is warmed from a lower temperature to a higher temperature while remaining entirely solid. What is the expected entropy trend?
options: Entropy cannot change unless melting occurs
Entropy decreases because the crystal contains the same atoms
Entropy becomes exactly zero at the warmer temperature
Entropy increases as energy becomes more dispersed within the solid.
questions.explanation: D is correct. A phase change is not required for heating to increase entropy. A is incorrect: energy redistribution can change entropy within one phase. B is incorrect: unchanged composition does not imply decreasing entropy. C is incorrect: a warmer solid does not lose all accessible thermal arrangements.

questions.prompt: Which process decreases the entropy of an ideal gas through both of the stated changes?
options: Heating and expanding the gas
Cooling and compressing the gas.
Heating at fixed volume
Isothermal expansion
questions.explanation: B is correct. Cooling reduces energy dispersal and compression reduces available spatial volume; both contributions lower gas entropy. A is incorrect: both changes tend to increase entropy. C is incorrect: this increases energy dispersal. D is incorrect: this increases spatial dispersal.

questions.prompt: For equal amounts of the same substance, why is vaporization generally associated with a larger entropy increase than melting?
options: Melting always has a negative entropy change
Vaporization destroys all atoms
Vaporization requires no energy dispersal
The transition to gas produces a much greater increase in spatial freedom.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Gas particles have far more accessible volume and arrangements than either condensed phase. A is incorrect: ordinary melting has positive entropy change. B is incorrect: it changes phase without destroying atoms. C is incorrect: both matter and energy dispersal contribute.

questions.prompt: For H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g), why is gas-mole counting alone insufficient to establish the entropy-change sign?
options: The total gas coefficient is unchanged, so molecular entropy data are needed for a reliable sign.
The reaction must have exactly zero entropy change
Balanced reactions cannot change entropy
Chlorine has no entropy because it is an element
questions.explanation: A is correct. Equal gas mole totals remove the strongest simple counting clue; species-specific entropies can still differ. B is incorrect: equal gas coefficients do not ensure equal entropy totals. C is incorrect: balanced equations conserve atoms, not entropy. D is incorrect: elements have nonzero standard molar entropy at ordinary temperatures.

questions.prompt: A liquid freezes at its transition temperature. Which statement correctly separates molecular identity from the entropy change?
options: Entropy stays constant whenever molecular formulas stay constant
The negative entropy change means matter is lost
The molecular identities can remain unchanged while the sample entropy decreases.
The solid must contain more independent gas particles
questions.explanation: C is correct. Freezing restricts particle arrangements without requiring a chemical transformation. A is incorrect: physical rearrangements and phase changes can change entropy. B is incorrect: entropy change does not measure loss of atoms. D is incorrect: freezing does not create a gas population.
